**Case Vignette: "Amir"**

Amir is a 54-year-old married man of Middle Eastern descent who presents for therapy at the urging of his wife, Layla. He is a well-respected community organizer in a mid-sized city, known for his calm demeanor and ability to mediate between rival factions. For the past three months, he has been unable to attend community meetings, canceling at the last minute with vague excuses about "feeling unwell." In session, he sits forward in his chair, hands clasped tightly, his voice low and measured.

The trauma Amir carries began two years ago, though he did not recognize it as such until recently. He was in a romantic relationship with a woman named Nadia, who was also a prominent activist in his network. Their relationship was intense and passionate, but privately volatile. Amir describes Nadia as "a force of nature" who could be both deeply loving and terrifyingly unpredictable. The physical abuse started gradually—a shove during an argument, a slap that he rationalized as "a mistake." He told himself he was strong enough to handle it, that her stress from work was to blame.

The defining event occurred on a rainy Tuesday evening. Amir had come home late from a city council meeting. Nadia was waiting, furious about a political disagreement they’d had earlier. He remembers her words: "You think you’re better than me." Then she picked up a heavy ceramic vase and struck him across the face. He fell to the floor, dazed, blood streaming from a gash above his eye. She did not stop. He recalls the sensation of her knee pressing into his chest, the sound of his own ribs cracking, the smell of her perfume mixed with his own blood. He did not fight back. "I froze," he says, his voice barely a whisper. "I just lay there and let it happen."

After the assault, Amir ended the relationship. He never reported it to the police. He told no one. He cleaned his own wounds, lied about the bruises, and returned to work three days later. He told himself the story was over.

But the story is not over. In the months since, Amir has become a prisoner in his own home. He cannot sit with his back to a door. When Layla raises her voice in frustration—even at a slow driver—Amir’s heart pounds, his vision narrows, and he feels a cold sweat break out on his palms. He has begun sleeping in the guest room, because he cannot tolerate the sensation of another body next to him in the dark. He avoids public spaces, particularly crowded restaurants, where he finds himself scanning every face, watching for sudden movements. His work, once his lifeblood, now feels impossible. He cannot sit through a contentious meeting without feeling a surge of panic, his mind flashing to the vase, the floor, the weight on his chest.

He has become hypervigilant toward women in positions of authority, a fact that shames him deeply. He knows it is unfair, but he cannot control the automatic dread that rises when a female colleague raises her voice or gestures emphatically. He has started avoiding certain female allies entirely, canceling one-on-one meetings at the last minute.

Amir’s sleep is fragmented by nightmares. He does not dream of Nadia’s face, but of being pinned, unable to move, while a heavy, formless weight presses down on his chest. He wakes gasping, drenched in sweat, often with his hands clenched into fists. He has begun drinking three to four glasses of whiskey each night, telling himself it is to "settle his nerves" before bed.

He is profoundly isolated. He cannot tell his community—the very people who see him as a pillar of strength—that he was beaten by a woman. The shame is a physical weight, heavier than the memory of the assault. He says, "I am supposed to be the one who protects. I am supposed to be the one who stands firm. I am a leader. How can I lead when I cannot even keep myself safe?"

In session, Amir is articulate and insightful, yet he holds himself as if bracing for a blow. He speaks of his past with a flat, detached tone, as if describing something that happened to someone else. His hands tremble slightly when he describes the moment he decided to leave Nadia. He looks at the therapist with a mixture of hope and profound exhaustion. He wants to be free, but he does not know how to begin.
